ANALOG ELECTRONICS • MULTISIM PROJECT

Design an Active Low-Pass Filter

A sensor signal contains high-frequency noise that must be attenuated before processing. This complete project page includes the Multisim circuit and output screenshots, theory, calculations, simulation procedure, viva questions, and GATE-style practice questions.

AimTheoryCircuitOutputProcedureVivaGATE MCQsResult
01 • Project aim

Aim and objectives

Aim: To design and simulate an op-amp active low-pass filter that passes low-frequency sensor signals and attenuates high-frequency noise.

Components from your circuit

  • OPAMP_5T_VIRTUAL
  • Function generator XFG1
  • R3 = 10 kΩ
  • R2 = 10 kΩ
  • C1 = 100 nF
  • Oscilloscope XSC1
  • VCC = +15 V and VEE = −15 V labels

Expected behaviour

Low-frequency signals should pass with little attenuation. As frequency rises above the cutoff frequency, output amplitude should reduce.

First-order low-pass filter
02 • Theory and calculation

Working principle

The resistor and capacitor form an RC low-pass network at the op-amp's non-inverting input. The op-amp stage buffers the filtered signal. The RC cutoff frequency is:

fc = 1 / (2πRC)

Using R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF:

fc = 1 / (2π × 10,000 × 100 × 10−9) ≈ 159.15 Hz
FrequencyExpected response of first-order RC stage
f ≪ fcMost of the signal passes
f = fcMagnitude is 0.707 of passband value (−3 dB)
f ≫ fcSignal is attenuated

The magnitude response of the RC stage is |H(jf)| = 1 / √(1 + (f/fc)²). Overall gain also depends on the op-amp wiring and feedback configuration.

05 • Simulation procedure

Multisim steps

  1. Open the circuit in Multisim.
  2. Confirm R3 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ and C1 = 100 nF.
  3. Check the op-amp supply pins use correct +15 V and −15 V polarities.
  4. Set the function generator to a sine wave and a small input amplitude within the op-amp's limits.
  5. Connect Channel A to the input and Channel B to the output, using a common ground reference.
  6. Run the circuit and observe both waveforms.
  7. Repeat at 20 Hz, approximately 159 Hz and 1 kHz; record input/output amplitudes.
  8. Compare the measurements with the expected low-pass response.
Test frequencyExpected observation
20 HzBelow cutoff: signal should mostly pass
159 HzNear cutoff: RC stage magnitude about 0.707 of passband
1 kHzAbove cutoff: signal should be attenuated
06 • Viva voce

Viva questions with answers

1. What is a low-pass filter?

A low-pass filter passes low-frequency signals and attenuates high-frequency signals.

2. Why is a low-pass filter used with a sensor?

It reduces unwanted high-frequency noise before the sensor signal is processed.

3. What is an active filter?

An active filter uses an active component, such as an op-amp, along with resistors and capacitors.

4. What is the role of the resistor?

The resistor works with the capacitor to determine the cutoff frequency.

5. What is the role of the capacitor?

Its impedance decreases as frequency increases, helping attenuate high-frequency components.

6. What is cutoff frequency?

The frequency where a first-order filter magnitude falls to about 0.707 of passband magnitude (−3 dB).

7. Write the cutoff-frequency formula.

fc = 1/(2πRC).

8. Calculate cutoff frequency for R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF.

fc ≈ 159.15 Hz.

9. What is the attenuation slope of a first-order low-pass filter?

Approximately −20 dB per decade, or −6 dB per octave, above cutoff.

10. What does −3 dB mean in voltage magnitude?

The output magnitude is approximately 0.707 times the passband magnitude.

11. Why is an op-amp used?

It can buffer the RC network and provide gain, depending on circuit configuration.

12. Difference between active and passive filters?

Active filters use active devices such as op-amps and can provide gain; passive filters use resistors, capacitors and/or inductors only.

13. What is the function of an oscilloscope?

It displays voltage waveforms versus time so input and output can be compared.

14. Why is a common ground needed?

It provides a shared voltage reference for the source, circuit and measuring instrument.

15. What happens when input frequency is much higher than cutoff?

The output amplitude is reduced compared with its passband value.

16. Give applications of a low-pass filter.

Sensor conditioning, noise reduction, audio processing, data acquisition and anti-alias filtering.

17. Why check op-amp supply connections?

Incorrect supplies can prevent correct operation or make the output saturate.

18. Why is simulation useful?

It helps verify circuit behaviour before building the physical circuit.

08 • Result

Observation and conclusion

  • R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF give an RC cutoff frequency of approximately 159.15 Hz.
  • The supplied Multisim circuit and oscilloscope screenshots are included.
  • For complete verification, test below, near and above cutoff and compare input/output amplitudes.
Accuracy note: The screenshot shows waveforms, but does not clearly state the function-generator frequency or a frequency sweep. To prove frequency response, record measurements at 20 Hz, approximately 159 Hz and 1 kHz.

Conclusion: An active low-pass filter can reduce high-frequency noise in a sensor signal. The theoretical cutoff frequency for the shown 10 kΩ and 100 nF RC values is approximately 159.15 Hz.
